finance#2.en:
Match the situation to the formula. i is the rate as a fraction (÷100), n the number of periods.

  • Hire purchase → simple interest: A = P(1 + i·n)
  • Inflation, population growth, savings → compound: A = P(1 + i)ⁿ
  • Straight-line depreciation → A = P(1 − i·n)
  • Reducing-balance depreciation → A = P(1 − i)ⁿ

P is the starting amount, A the end amount. Turn a % into i by dividing by 100 (8% → 0,08).

finance#4.en:
Simple interest is worked out on the original P only, so the same amount is added each period.

A = P(1 + i·n)

Compound interest is worked out on the growing balance, so each period earns a little more than the last.

A = P(1 + i)ⁿ
Over time compound always pulls ahead of simple, because it earns "interest on interest".

finance#6.en:
Depreciation is when something loses value over time.

  • Linear (straight-line): A = P(1 − i·n). Loses the same rand amount each year — its graph is a straight line sloping down.
  • Reducing-balance: A = P(1 − i)ⁿ. Loses a fixed percentage of its current value each year — its graph is a curve that drops steeply then flattens.

finance#8.en:
If interest is added more than once a year, split the year up:

  • rate per period = annual rate ÷ (times per year)
  • exponent = years × (times per year)
A = P(1 + i/k)n·k

Times per year k: annually 1 · half‑yearly 2 · quarterly 4 · monthly 12 · weekly 52 · daily 365.

12% p.a. compounded quarterly for 5 years → i = 0,12/4 = 0,03 and exponent = 5×4 = 20.

finance#10.en:
Money has a different value at different times. To re-value an amount, slide it along the timeline:

  • Forward (to a later date) → multiply by (1 + i) once per period → a positive exponent.
  • Backward (to an earlier date) → divide by (1 + i) once per period → a negative exponent.
value = amount × (1 + i)±periods

Count the periods between the two T‑points. Forward T2 → T5 is 3 periods (+3); backward T5 → T2 is 3 periods (−3).

finance#12.en:
The number of periods is just how many gaps you jump between the two T‑points — count the spaces, not the dots.

  • T0 → T4 is 4 periods.
  • T5 → T2 is 3 periods (going back).

The direction tells you × or ÷: later = ×, earlier = ÷.

finance#14.en:
If the rate or compounding frequency changes part-way, split the timeline into segments. For a single amount, use one bracket per segment:

A = P(1 + i₁/k₁)n₁·k₁ (1 + i₂/k₂)n₂·k₂

Work out each segment's rate-per-period and number-of-periods separately, then multiply the brackets together.

finance#16.en:
A deposit is paid upfront and earns no interest.

deposit = (% ÷ 100) × price

The amount still owed (the new P that interest is charged on) is the rest of the price:

amount owed = ((100 − %) ÷ 100) × price
15% deposit on R8 000 → deposit = R1 200, still owed = R6 800.

finance#18.en:
Both are compound interest, just quoted differently.

  • Effective rate is always an annual rate (the true yearly growth).
  • Nominal rate is quoted with a compounding frequency (monthly, quarterly, …).
1 + ieff = (1 + inomn)ⁿ

Here n is the number of compounding periods per year (12 for monthly).

finance#19.en: Payments are coins. The total is the jug.

finance#20.en:
Every payment is one coin going in or out on its day. The total (the lumpsum) is the one jug all the coins are worth together. A coin is never the jug. Your textbook says “lump sum”. That is the total we are talking about. From now on we just call it the total.

${JUG_PICTURE}

Interest makes the jug grow (or the debt grow). A withdrawal takes a coin out. The jug can end up smaller than a coin: it is still the jug.

finance#22.en:
Every amount on a timeline is moved to one T, the meeting day (the flag on the line).

A car is the bracket (1 + i)n that moves an amount to the meeting day.

  • Forward gear: the meeting day is later, so multiply (×): a positive exponent.
  • Reverse gear: the meeting day is earlier, so divide (÷): a negative exponent.
  • An amount already standing on the meeting day needs no car.
  • Each road is one rate, in one colour. Where the road changes colour, the rate changes: an amount that crosses it needs one car per road.
exponent = ± years × k

k is how many times a year the interest is added: annually 1 · half‑yearly 2 · quarterly 4 · monthly 12.

8% p.a. compounded quarterly until T4, then 10% p.a. compounded monthly. R5 000 at T2, meeting day T6: two cars, both forward: 5 000(1 + 0,08/4)2×4 (1 + 0,1/12)2×12.
Her last deposit, R2 000, is paid in on the same day as A, and the meeting day is that day: no car, it is just 2 000.

A car only if it has to move. Already there? No car.

finance#24.en:
Every amount on the timeline drives to the meeting day in its car (a car is the (1 + i)n bracket that moves an amount to the meeting day). The meeting day is the total's own day, so the total stands alone on the left, with no car. Every other amount goes on the right, with its sign.

  • Saving: the total is A, at the end. A deposit goes IN: + on the right. A withdrawal comes OUT: − on the right. On a timeline a withdrawal is drawn −R2 000.
  • A loan: the loan goes in too, but it is the total, P, at T0: it stands alone on the left. Every repayment goes + on the right, driving back to T0 in reverse gear.
  • A down payment never enters the account: it is paid straight to the seller, so it has no place in the equation. It comes off the price: loan = price − down payment.
Saving with a withdrawal: R14 000 in at T0, R2 000 out at T3, 8% p.a. compounded quarterly, A at T5, the meeting day: A = 14 000(1 + 0,08/4)20 − 2 000(1 + 0,08/4)8
A loan paid back with R8 000 at T1 and R9 000 at T3, 12% p.a. compounded monthly, meeting day T0: P = 8 000(1 + 0,12/12)−12 + 9 000(1 + 0,12/12)−36

Interest on a loan = paid back − borrowed.

Saving: deposits plus, withdrawals minus, A alone on the left. A loan: repayments plus on the right, P alone on the left.

finance#26.en:
The exam hands you words. Build the whole timeline from them, tap by tap, before any equation. Every payment is one coin on its day; the total is the one jug.

  • Tap 1: how far does it go? The last day the words name is the last T: “after 7 years” is T7.
  • Tap 2: where does the rate change? “for the first 3 years” is T3. One rate all the way: no change.
  • Tap 3: which rate on which road? The first rate from T0 to the change, the new rate after it, each road in its own colour.
  • Tap 4: where does the jug go? Savings: at the end, A. A loan: at T0, P.
  • Tap 5: where does each coin go? “now” is T0, “after 5 years” is T5; a coin going out is drawn −R2 000.

A down payment never enters the account: it goes straight to the shop, so it has no place on the timeline.

Brenda opens a savings account. She deposits R5 500 now and R4 000 after 5 years. The interest rate is 14% p.a. compounded half‑yearly for the first 3 years, then 12% p.a. compounded monthly. How much is in the account after 7 years?

The five taps: T7; T3; 14% p.a., then 12% p.a.; the jug, A, at T7; R5 500 at T0 and R4 000 at T5.

${renderTimeline(BUILD_TIMELINE_EXAMPLE)}
T in years

Words first. Then the timeline. Then the one equation.

finance#28.en:
• Step 1: pick the meeting day. Saving: the day of A, at the end. A loan: T0, the day of the loan.
  • Step 2: give every amount its car (a car is the (1 + i)n bracket that moves an amount to the meeting day). Forward gear to a later day: a positive exponent. Reverse gear to an earlier day: a negative exponent. One car per road. An amount already standing on the meeting day gets no car.
  • Step 3: write it all in ONE line. The total alone on the left (A for saving, the loan P for a loan). The payments on the right: a deposit or a repayment plus, a withdrawal minus.
  • Step 4: type it once, round once. Never solve it in stages and never round along the way: the answer to 2 decimal places, at the end.
Saving: R5 500 now and R4 000 at T5; 14% p.a. compounded half‑yearly for 3 years, then 12% p.a. compounded monthly; meeting day T7: A = 5 500(1 + 0,14/2)6 (1 + 0,12/12)48 + 4 000(1 + 0,12/12)24, so A = R18 386,28.
A loan paid off with R5 000 at T4 and R6 000 at T6; 16% p.a. compounded quarterly for 4 years, then 14% p.a. compounded half‑yearly; meeting day T0: P = 5 000(1 + 0,16/4)−16 + 6 000(1 + 0,14/2)−4 (1 + 0,16/4)−16, so P = R5 113,44.

The total is known and a payment is the unknown (a deposit P now, or x in the middle)? Write the same one line, the known total alone on the left, and let SHIFT SOLVE find the unknown.

A down payment never enters the loan: it comes off the price. Price = loan + down payment.

Build the whole equation first. Type it once. Round once, at the end.

finance#30.en:
Any T can be the meeting day. Every amount drives there in its car (a car is the (1 + i)n bracket that moves an amount to the meeting day), the total too when it is not already there. Count the cars for a day:

  • An amount already standing on the meeting day: no car.
  • An amount that stays on one colour of road: 1 car.
  • An amount that crosses the colour change: 2 cars, one per road.

Two rules of thumb for the day with the fewest cars:

  • Meet where someone already stands. That amount needs no car.
  • Meet where the road changes colour. Then nobody crosses the change, so nobody needs two cars.
Saving: R5 000 at T1, R3 000 at T3, A at T6; 8% p.a. until T3, then 10% p.a., so the road changes colour at T3. Meet at T6: the R5 000 crosses the change (2 cars), the R3 000 needs 1 car, A is already there: 2 + 1 + 0 = 3 cars. Meet at T3: 1 + 0 + 1 = 2 cars. T3 does both: an amount stands there, and the road changes colour there.

The answer is the same wherever you meet; picking the day is only about typing less.
